passage:
Dear Damini,
You asked why I crossed the road yesterday when the constable was standing at the corner. Honest answer: since I saw an officer shove the fruit-seller near our market last month, every uniform feels like a warning. I tense up before anyone has done anything. But yesterday I watched that same constable for a while. He walked a lost old woman to the bus stand and held the traffic for her. That doesn't cancel what I saw, and I'll still be careful. But I don't want to treat everyone as a threat when some are doing their job properly. I'm still working it out. Tell me what you think.
Tanvir

qa.q: What did Tanvir see an officer do last month?
qa.a: Tanvir saw an officer shove the fruit-seller near the market.

qa.q: How does Tanvir feel about uniforms, and how is that feeling shifting?
qa.a: Tanvir tenses up at every uniform as if it were a warning, but seeing the constable help a lost old woman makes Tanvir unwilling to treat everyone as a threat.

qa.q: How can Tanvir stay careful without hating everyone?
qa.a: By judging each officer by what they actually do, staying alert and polite, and remembering that one bad moment is not every officer.

qa.q: How might Damini feel on receiving this letter?
qa.a: Probably trusted and thoughtful, since Tanvir shares a hard feeling openly and asks what Damini thinks.

grounding: After seeing bad police behaviour Tanvir sees every uniform as a threat, then starts to stay careful without hating everyone.

passage:
Durga Puja night in Kolkata, and the pandal crowd was so thick Binita could barely breathe. Then she looked down, and her little brother Lokesh's hand wasn't in hers anymore.

She screamed his name. Nothing. Phone battery dead. Her parents were at the other pandal across the road.

The only help nearby was a police help desk with two officers in khaki. Binita's feet stopped. Last year, near their lane, she had seen a constable kick a vegetable seller's basket over and slap him. Since then, every uniform looked like that man.

But Lokesh was six.

She pushed through and said, voice shaking, "My brother is lost. He's six, wearing a yellow kurta."

The woman officer didn't hesitate. She announced it on the loudspeaker and radioed the next booth. Eleven minutes later, a constable carried Lokesh over, sticky with candy floss.

Binita hugged him hard. She thanked the officer. On the way home she thought: that man last year, and this woman tonight. Both real.

qa.a: Lokesh was wearing a yellow kurta.

qa.q: Why did Binita's feet stop when she saw the police help desk?
qa.a: Binita felt afraid and distrustful, because she had seen a constable kick a basket and slap a vegetable seller the year before.

qa.q: What did Binita do that was wise in this moment?
qa.a: Binita put her brother's safety first, went to the police desk anyway and gave clear details, while keeping her own memory of past harm.

qa.q: How might the woman officer see Binita's shaking voice?
qa.a: The officer probably saw a frightened sister who needed help fast, which is why she acted at once.

grounding: It shows a teen who has seen bad police behaviour and distrusts every uniform, learning to stay careful without hating everyone when officers help find her brother.

passage:
Ishita still remembered the raid. Two years ago, police had turned her uncle's electronics shop in Karol Bagh upside down, shouting, knocking things off shelves, and found nothing. Since then, a khaki uniform made her chest go tight.

So when her school announced a road safety talk by a sub-inspector, she sat at the back with her arms crossed.

The officer turned out to be her classmate Francis's father. He talked about helmets and zebra crossings, and then about the teenager he'd pulled out of a crushed scooter last winter. His voice went rough for a moment.

Afterwards, Francis said, "You looked like you hated him the whole time."

"Not him," Ishita said slowly. "I just… I've seen police be awful."

"Yeah. Some are." Francis shrugged. "Papa says that too. He also sits up at night when his juniors do something wrong."

Ishita uncrossed her arms. She didn't feel like trusting every uniform. But she no longer wanted to hate every one either.

qa.a: Ishita's uncle's shop was in Karol Bagh.

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling at the start of the talk?
qa.a: Ishita felt tense and distrustful, with a tight chest, because of the raid on her uncle's shop.

qa.q: What shift in Ishita's thinking is healthy, and why?
qa.a: Ishita stays careful but no longer wants to hate every uniform, which lets her see individual officers fairly without forgetting real harm.

qa.q: How does Francis see his father's work?
qa.a: Francis sees that some police behave badly, but knows his father cares about doing the job properly and is troubled when his juniors do wrong.

grounding: It shows a teen who distrusts all police after seeing bad behaviour, learning to stay careful without hating everyone and seeing that many officers do their duty properly.
